name: Cree-Montagnais-Naskapi Continuum

formality.description: Cree languages do not have a European-style T-V distinction. Formality is expressed through respectful particles, verb forms, and lexical choices. The register system is shared across the continuum but specific vocabulary and orthography differ by variety.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Cree languages use an animacy distinction (animate vs inanimate noun classes) rather than grammatical gender. Verb conjugation, demonstratives, and plural marking all depend on animacy class.

variables.guidance: Variables are marked with braces `{count}`. Since Cree relies heavily on affixation, suffixes must attach directly to placeholders. Use a hyphen to separate the variable from grammatical affixes (e.g., `{count}-ak` or `{count}-a` for plurals).

linguisticChallenges.polysynthesis: All Cree varieties are highly polysynthetic. A single verb can incorporate subject/object pronouns, instrumentals, locations, and actions. Translate phrases conceptually rather than word-for-word.
linguisticChallenges.animacy: Verb conjugation changes completely based on whether the subject/object nouns are animate or inanimate. Ensure grammatical agreement. Animacy class is not always intuitive — e.g., 'rock' (asiniy) is animate.
linguisticChallenges.obviation: Cree uses a proximate/obviative system to track third-person referents. In discourse with multiple third persons, one is proximate (main) and others are obviative (secondary). MT systems frequently mishandle this.
linguisticChallenges.neologisms: Avoid literal translations of modern software concepts. Maintain English loanwords for modern UI elements when no community-accepted term exists. Each variety may coin different neologisms.
linguisticChallenges.dialectContinuum: The Cree-Montagnais-Naskapi varieties form a dialect continuum. Adjacent varieties are mutually intelligible; distant ones are not. Do NOT mix vocabulary from different varieties.

contactInfluences.period: fur trade era and missionary contact (17th–19th century)
contactInfluences.notes: French missionaries developed early Cree writing systems. French loanwords in eastern varieties (Innu, Atikamekw) are more numerous than in western varieties.
English is the dominant language of administration across all Cree territories. Code-switching is pervasive in younger speakers.
Southwestern Cree varieties (Plains, Swampy) share significant vocabulary with Ojibwe. The languages are closely related within Algonquian.

notes: Genus card for the Cree-Montagnais-Naskapi continuum. Individual variety cards (crk, csw, cwd, crm, crl, crj, atj, moe, nsk) extend this card and override with variety-specific data. macrolanguage is intentionally null here: only crj/crk/crl/crm/csw/cwd are ISO 639-3 members of the 'cre' macrolanguage (see cre.json members[]), and atj/moe/nsk/crg must not inherit a membership ISO does not assert. Members carry their own explicit macrolanguage field.
